name: Athas
tagline: A lightweight desktop code editor with AI editing baked into the buffer.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified, and the project may be free or open source with optional bring-your-own-key AI.

verdictSummary: An agent will happily hand you a window with a file tree, tabs and syntax highlighting before lunch, and you will feel briefly powerful. Then you open a 40MB log, hit a broken LSP restart, discover your undo stack forgets multi-cursor edits, and go back to whatever you were using. Editors are not a feature list, they are a decade of small correctnesses under keyboard latency pressure. The AI part is genuinely the easy half: it is a prompt, a diff, and an accept button. The editor around it is the hard half, and one session does not buy it.
coreLoopDIY: A local desktop editor that opens a folder, edits files in tabs with syntax highlighting and fuzzy search, and applies AI-suggested diffs you accept or reject.
requirements: Rust toolchain and Node for Tauri
a language server binary on PATH for whatever language you care about
an LLM API key in .env if you want the AI editing loop
willingness to keep patching it forever
whatYouLose: Language intelligence that actually holds up: rename across files, go to definition in generated code, diagnostics that do not lag
Performance discipline on huge files, huge repos and huge diffs
An extension ecosystem, or even a plausible imitation of one
Git integration beyond a status list, meaning real staging, hunks and conflict resolution
Keybinding and command palette muscle memory that took you years to build
moatNotes: Editors compete on latency and on how rarely they surprise you, which is exactly the kind of quality that does not fall out of a single generation pass.
whyPeopleStillPay: Mostly people do not pay much for editors, they pay with attachment: the thing that opens in 300ms, remembers their layout, and does not eat a keystroke during a refactor earns loyalty that money cannot shortcut. If there is a paid tier here it is buying the AI loop and the maintenance, not the text field. The honest reason to stay on a real editor is that your editor is the one tool where a 2% annoyance rate is unbearable, and a DIY build starts around 40%.
notes: An agent can produce a window with syntax colors and an AI diff panel in an afternoon, and it will be fun for an afternoon. The moat is the thousand small correctnesses: language server edge cases, large file handling, git hunks, and keystroke latency you never think about until it is gone.
prompt:
Build a local desktop code editor called Scratchpad. No accounts, no telemetry, no cloud sync.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Tauri v2 shell, Rust backend.
- React + TypeScript + Vite frontend.
- CodeMirror 6 for the editor surface.
- ripgrep shelled out from Rust for project search.
- Zustand for UI state. Tailwind for styling. No component library.

Features in scope:
1. Open a folder. Persist the last folder and open tabs in a local JSON file under the app data dir.
2. Virtualized file tree with create, rename, delete, and gitignore-aware filtering.
3. Tabbed editing with dirty indicators, Cmd+S save, Cmd+W close, and a real undo history per tab.
4. Syntax highlighting for TypeScript, JavaScript, JSON, Rust, Python, Markdown via CodeMirror language packages.
5. Command palette (Cmd+K) and fuzzy file open (Cmd+P) over a cached file index.
6. Project-wide search panel using ripgrep, results grouped by file, click to jump to line.
7. One language server: spawn typescript-language-server over stdio from Rust, wire diagnostics, hover, and go-to-definition only. Log and recover from crashes, do not pretend the protocol is simple.
8. AI edit: select code, Cmd+I, type an instruction, send file context to an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, render the response as a unified diff in a side panel with accept-hunk and reject-hunk buttons. Key from .env as AI_API_KEY, base URL as AI_BASE_URL. Never send anything if the key is missing.

Out of scope, do not build: extensions, integrated terminal, debugger, git UI beyond showing changed-file badges, remote development, themes beyond one dark and one light.

Deliverables: working `pnpm tauri dev`, a README with keybindings and known limitations, and a .env.example. Write the file-index and diff-apply logic with unit tests, since those are where the data loss lives.
